entities.name: Byzantine Empire under the Theodosian dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Byzantine Empire under the Theodosian dynasty (379-457 CE) governed the final decades of the unified Roman Empire and the first generation of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, presiding over Christianity's establishment as the Roman state religion, the first permanent division of the empire, and the dramatic fall of the Western Roman Empire. Theodosius I (r. 379-395 CE) was the last ruler of the unified empire: his 380 CE Edict of Thessalonica made Nicene Christianity the sole legal religion of the Roman Empire — the most consequential act of religious legislation in Western history.

Theodosius I's 391 CE prohibition of all pagan cults (temple closures, cessation of Olympic Games, end of the Vestal Virgins) ended 1,200 years of Roman polytheism and permanently transformed Western civilization's religious character. His 394 CE final victory over the pagan usurper Eugenius was the last battle between paganism and Christianity for control of the Roman state. When Theodosius died in 395 CE, he divided the empire between his sons Arcadius (East) and Honorius (West) — a division that became permanent.

Under the Theodosian dynasty's Eastern successors, the Western Roman Empire collapsed: Honorius's court at Ravenna did nothing as Alaric sacked Rome (410 CE) and the Vandals sacked it again (455 CE); the last Western emperor Romulus Augustulus was deposed by Odoacer in 476 CE. The Eastern Empire under Theodosius II (r. 408-450 CE) built the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople (413 CE) — the most formidable defensive walls in Western history, preserving the city for 1,000 more years — and commissioned the Theodosian Code (438 CE), the first systematic codification of Roman law.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Theodosian dynasty — establishing Christianity as Rome's state religion (380 CE), ending 1,200 years of Roman polytheism, presiding over the Western Empire's fall (476 CE), and building Constantinople's walls that preserved it for 1,000 years — governed the most transformative generation in Western religious and political history.
